title: Request Concierge: tiered qualification and delivery lanes for console analytics asks
creator: Ava Chen
description: Background: Enterprise customers frequently submit a wide variety of console and reporting requests (ad-hoc usage exports, tenant-aware cost breakdowns, custom dashboards, and scheduled slices). Today these requests land in a single intake queue which creates long lead times, unclear SLAs, and repeated back-and-forth with customers to scope deliverables. Problem: Lack of a standardized qualification rubric causes inconsistent prioritization and inefficient routing between self-serve, platform, and engineering-assisted teams. Consequence: high-touch requests block small triage resources, predictable work is deprioritized, and customers experience opaque timelines. Goal: Define a 'Request Concierge'—a lightweight qualification and routing layer that classifies incoming console/reporting asks into tiered delivery lanes with clear SLAs, templated scoping forms, and automation for routing and acceptance. The concierge should reduce manual triage overhead, reduce time-to-first-response for enterprise customers, and increase throughput for low-effort requests via self-serve tooling.
proposed_solution: 1) Intake form overhaul: create a single canonical 'Console Analytics Request' form with enforced fields (use case, tenant scope, data ranges, export format, desired cadence, urgency, customer tier, examples). 2) Qualification rubric: automated scoring that maps requests to lanes: 'Self-Serve' (auto-approved, docs + templates), 'Concierge' (PM/solutions engineer scoping + scheduled delivery within 7 business days), 'Engineering-Assisted' (requires ENG work, SLA based on priority). 3) Delivery lanes and SLAs: define SLAs per lane (e.g., Self-Serve: 0-2 business days; Concierge: 3-10 business days; Eng-Assisted: kickoff within 5 business days, ETA provided). 4) Routing automation: integrate with Linear/GH labels + JIRA-like project board so form responses create PM- or ENG- prefixed issues with metadata and suggested acceptance criteria. 5) Templates & runbook: canned SQL/report templates, standard cost-breakdown schemas, dashboard skeletons, and a published concierge runbook for support/solutions teams. 6) Backstop & escalation: define fallback to canary exports or scheduled snapshots for data-heavy requests and documented escalation path to account lead or SRE for performance/regulatory constraints.
acceptance_criteria: Canonical intake form lives in console and requires key scoping fields before submission
Automated rubric assigns > 90% of incoming requests to a lane without manual editing during pilot
Self-Serve lane has at least three published templates (usage export, cost-breakdown, dashboard start) with documentation
Concierge lane SLA defined and measured: 90th percentile time-to-first-delivery <= 10 business days during pilot
Routing automation creates Linear issues with correct labels and suggested acceptance criteria for each lane
Metrics dashboard tracks intake volume, lane distribution, time-to-first-response, and customer satisfaction for requests
rollout_plan: Week 1: Draft intake form + rubric; align with Solutions, Support, and Sales on required fields
Week 2: Build wireframe in Console and prototype automation to create Linear issues; publish initial templates
Week 3: Run 2-week pilot with three enterprise accounts (opt-in); collect telemetry and feedback
Week 4: Iterate on rubric thresholds and templates; add two additional templates for scheduled exports
Week 5: Broad rollout for all enterprise workspaces; enable routing automation and dashboarding for SLAs
metrics: Percent of requests auto-classified by rubric
Number of requests resolved via Self-Serve templates
Customer satisfaction (post-request NPS) for Concierge lane
Average ENG hours per Eng-Assisted request
notes: Trade-offs: stricter intake fields reduce friction but may increase initial drop-off; will monitor abandonment rate and add inline help.
We will prioritize creating templates for the three most common asks observed in last 6 months: tenant-level cost breakdowns, scheduled usage exports, and per-route token breakdowns.
Privacy/regulatory: some exports may require Private deployment/connector review—add flag in form to trigger security review for air-gapped or regulated customers.
